heuristics.rule: Don't negotiate an internal promotion without an external offer unless you're willing to accept a slower, weaker outcome
heuristics.condition: When pursuing an internal promotion salary negotiation...
heuristics.action: ...obtain a real competing external offer before initiating the negotiation
heuristics.because: Without an external offer, the company knows your reservation price, the status quo is the default, and managers can delay or partially deliver without consequences

heuristics.rule: Negotiate promotion compensation before accepting the promotion, not after
heuristics.condition: When a company signals they are considering you for an internal promotion...
heuristics.action: ...say 'I'd like to discuss compensation for the new level' before the promotion is finalized
heuristics.because: Once you've accepted the promotion, your leverage disappears — the company has already achieved their goal of keeping you in the new role

heuristics.rule: Anchor internal promotion comp on market rate for the new role, not your current salary
heuristics.condition: When negotiating pay for an internal promotion...
heuristics.action: ...research and cite market comp for the new role level using external sources like levels.fyi
heuristics.because: Internal hires are systematically offered below market on the assumption they're 'already paid' — reframing to the new role's market rate counters this bias

heuristics.rule: Do not accept a retention counter-offer unless the root cause of your dissatisfaction is resolved, not just compensated
heuristics.condition: When a company makes a retention counter-offer after you reveal an external offer...
heuristics.action: ...ask yourself 'If this job paid what they're now offering, would I have stayed?' and decline if the answer is no
heuristics.because: 80% of people who accept retention counter-offers still leave within 12 months, and the counter-offer typically only buys the company time to find your replacement

heuristics.rule: Negotiate internal transfer compensation at the time of transfer, not after proving yourself
heuristics.condition: When accepting an internal transfer to a new team or role...
heuristics.action: ...explicitly negotiate a comp increase reflecting the scope change before agreeing to the transfer
heuristics.because: Post-transfer, your leverage drops to near zero — you're now in the new role and the company has achieved their staffing goal

heuristics.rule: Calculate the hidden promo clock cost before accepting any internal transfer at the same level
heuristics.condition: When evaluating an internal transfer offer at your current level mid-promo-cycle...
heuristics.action: ...calculate total months added to your next promotion eligibility (months elapsed + new 12–18 month clock)
heuristics.because: An internal transfer at the same level can push your next promotion 2+ years away, representing a significant hidden compensation and career cost

heuristics.rule: Request a market correction off-cycle when documented comp gap exceeds roughly 20%
heuristics.condition: When you have clear market data showing your comp is significantly below median and your performance is strong...
heuristics.action: ...explicitly request a 'market correction' discussion rather than waiting for annual review
heuristics.because: Most companies have off-cycle adjustment mechanisms for documented gaps, but they are rarely proactively offered — you must initiate

heuristics.rule: Present an external offer with explicit preference to stay, then state the number
heuristics.condition: When using an external offer as leverage in an internal negotiation...
heuristics.action: ...frame it as 'I received an offer I'm seriously considering — I'd prefer to stay and wanted to give you the chance to respond before I decide,' then name the number
heuristics.because: This framing removes adversarial tone, signals genuine openness to staying, and forces a concrete, time-bounded decision from the company

heuristics.rule: Nail down promotion criteria and timeline in writing before negotiating comp
heuristics.condition: When a promotion is discretionary and not yet formally approved...
heuristics.action: ...secure written criteria and timeline for the promotion before discussing compensation
heuristics.because: A verbal promise of promotion has no enforceability; written criteria creates accountability and prevents indefinite deferral

decision_factors.factor: Presence of a real external competing offer
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Transforms internal negotiation leverage from low to high by introducing a credible, time-bounded cost of inaction for the employer
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Do you have a written offer with a specific number and deadline? A verbal interest or recruiter reach-out does not constitute real leverage

decision_factors.factor: Root cause of considering a move
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether a retention counter-offer can actually resolve your dissatisfaction or just delay inevitable departure
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask: 'If comp were fixed, would I still want to leave?' If yes due to manager, scope, learning, or ceiling — comp alone won't fix it

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines the true hidden cost of an internal transfer at the same level — it can add 2+ years to your next promotion eligibility
decision_factors.how_to_assess: How many months into your current promo cycle are you? What is the company's minimum tenure before next promotion after a transfer?

decision_factors.factor: Whether promotion is discretionary vs. criteria-based
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Discretionary promotions are subject to indefinite deferral; criteria-based promotions give you something concrete to negotiate around and hold the company accountable to
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask your manager: 'What specifically would I need to demonstrate, and by when, to get promoted?' Vague answers indicate discretionary

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether emergency retention budget exists and whether a market correction request will be taken seriously
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Is the company growing or in downsizing mode? Have you seen colleagues successfully negotiate off-cycle adjustments?

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Even a willing manager may be structurally unable to approve above-band comp — understanding band limits sets realistic expectations
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask HR or your manager directly: 'What is the band for this role/level?' Some companies share this openly; others require indirect research

decision_factors.factor: Unvested equity and bonus proration impact of a transfer
decision_factors.why_it_matters: An internal transfer may affect unvested equity vesting schedules or bonus eligibility, representing real hidden comp loss
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Review your equity grant schedule and bonus plan terms; ask HR explicitly how a transfer affects both

decision_factors.factor: Quality of market comp data available
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Objective external anchors like levels.fyi or competing offers make negotiation concrete and harder to dismiss — without them, the negotiation is subjective
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Do you have recent, role-specific, level-specific data points with sample sizes? Single data points are weak; patterns across multiple sources are strong

decision_factors.factor: Whether you've already revealed you're looking
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Revealing that you're job searching changes your relationship with your employer regardless of whether you stay — it signals flight risk and can affect future opportunities
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Have you told your manager, HR, or skip-level that you've been interviewing or received an offer?

hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The company now knows you're a flight risk and may deprioritize you for promotions, key projects, or new responsibilities while quietly searching for your replacement
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: People who accepted for comp reasons while the root cause was scope, manager fit, or career ceiling — they stay but the dynamic is permanently altered

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Taking an internal transfer at the same level mid-promo-cycle
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Your promotion eligibility clock resets, potentially pushing your next promotion 2+ years out even though you accepted what looked like a lateral move
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High performers who are 6–12 months into a promo cycle and don't calculate the full timeline cost before accepting

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating for internal promotion without an external offer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Manager can delay with vague promises ('we'll make it right at your next review') with no accountability, and you're locked in mid-cycle unable to credibly threaten to leave
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Loyal employees who prefer stability and haven't maintained external market optionality

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Revealing an external offer to your current employer
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Even if you stay via counter-offer, you've permanently signaled disloyalty — future career advancement may be quietly impeded
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: People who use the external offer as a negotiation tactic but genuinely intend to stay long-term

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Waiting for the annual review cycle to address a significant comp gap
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Comp gaps compound over time — a 20% underpayment left unaddressed for 2–3 years becomes structural underpayment that's harder to correct in a single cycle
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High performers at companies with modest annual raise percentages who don't proactively request off-cycle market corrections

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a promotion verbally without written criteria or comp terms
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The promotion can be delayed, rescoped, or undercompensated with no recourse — verbal promises have no enforceability when managers change or budgets shift
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Employees who trust manager relationships and don't formalize agreements in writing

failure_patterns.pattern: Negotiating internal promotion compensation after accepting the promotion
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: People feel grateful for being chosen and don't want to seem ungrateful or risk having the offer rescinded — they accept first, then try to negotiate
failure_patterns.consequence: Leverage is gone once the promotion is accepted; the company has achieved their goal and has little incentive to increase comp beyond what they already offered
warning_signs: Saying 'thank you so much, I'm excited — can we also talk about comp?' after verbally accepting
Feeling like raising comp would seem greedy after being promoted

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting a retention counter-offer when the root cause was not compensation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Money is tangible and immediate; the real reasons for dissatisfaction (bad manager, no scope, stagnation) are harder to quantify and easier to temporarily rationalize away
failure_patterns.consequence: 80% of people who accept retention counter-offers leave within 12 months anyway — you've burned the external opportunity and damaged your internal relationship
warning_signs: Telling yourself 'the money makes it worth staying' while knowing the job itself hasn't changed
Feeling relief at the counter-offer without feeling excited about the work

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating a verbal promotion promise as binding without written criteria
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Employees trust their manager relationship and don't want to appear distrustful by asking for things in writing
failure_patterns.consequence: Promotions get delayed indefinitely, criteria shift, managers change — the employee has no accountability mechanism and loses months or years of career progression
warning_signs: Manager says 'you're on track' but can't specify what 'on track' means
Promotion timeline keeps slipping with new reasons each cycle

failure_patterns.pattern: Not calculating the promo clock impact before accepting an internal transfer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The promo clock reset is not prominently disclosed during transfer conversations — employees focus on role scope and immediate comp, not multi-year promotion trajectory
failure_patterns.consequence: A seemingly neutral lateral move delays the next promotion by 2+ years, representing significant lost comp and seniority
warning_signs: Accepting a transfer at the same level without asking 'does this reset my promotion eligibility?'
Assuming the new team will count your prior tenure toward promotion

failure_patterns.pattern: Anchoring internal promotion negotiations on current salary rather than market rate for the new role
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Both employee and employer default to 'what you're making now plus a percentage' framing — it's the path of least resistance and feels fair
failure_patterns.consequence: Employee gets locked in below market for the new role level, and the underpayment compounds with each subsequent annual increase
warning_signs: Thinking 'a 10% raise seems reasonable for a promotion'
Not researching market comp for the new role before the conversation

failure_patterns.pattern: Using an external offer as leverage without being genuinely prepared to take it
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: People generate an offer to gain negotiating power but haven't fully decided — they reveal the offer but fold when the company makes any counter, signaling they were bluffing
failure_patterns.consequence: Company learns you're a flight risk but not a credible one — future negotiations are weakened and you may be deprioritized
warning_signs: Getting an offer just to have 'something to show' without serious evaluation of taking it
Feeling relieved when the company counters so you don't have to decide

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a real, written external offer with a specific number and deadline?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you have actual leverage in the internal negotiation or are negotiating from comfort
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Are you genuinely willing to take the external offer if the company doesn't match? If not, your leverage is partially a bluff
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Is obtaining an external offer feasible before your internal negotiation window? If not, shift strategy to market data and business case framing

diagnostic_questions.question: If your current job paid exactly what you're asking for, would you still want to stay?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the dissatisfaction is purely compensation or driven by scope, manager, team, or career ceiling
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Then a retention counter-offer addresses the root cause — evaluate whether the comp offered is competitive
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Then money alone won't fix the problem — a retention counter-offer buys time but not satisfaction; evaluate the external offer on its full merits

diagnostic_questions.question: How many months into your current promotion cycle are you?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: The true hidden cost of accepting an internal transfer at the same level — the more time elapsed, the more a clock reset costs you
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If 6+ months in, calculate: months elapsed + new promo clock length to understand total delay before negotiating transfer terms
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If early in cycle, the promo clock impact is smaller but still worth quantifying and negotiating compensation for

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the promotion discretionary or criteria-based?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you have anything concrete to hold the company accountable to, or whether you're dependent entirely on manager goodwill
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If criteria-based, get the specific criteria and timeline in writing before any comp discussion
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If discretionary, prioritize converting vague promises into written criteria before negotiating comp — otherwise the promotion itself is at risk of indefinite deferral

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you already told your employer you're considering leaving or received an external offer?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you've permanently altered the employment relationship and what risks come with the current path
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: You're now in retention negotiation mode — be clear-eyed about whether the root cause can be addressed, not just compensated
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: You still have full optionality — decide whether to use the external offer as leverage internally or simply take it externally

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the internal transfer affect your unvested equity or bonus eligibility?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: The total real compensation cost of the transfer beyond just base salary and promo clock
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Quantify the unvested equity value and bonus impact; negotiate transfer terms that account for this loss
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Confirm this explicitly in writing with HR before accepting — vague assurances are not binding

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your company in a growth and retention posture or a cost-reduction and downsizing mode?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether emergency retention budget exists and whether a market correction request will be taken seriously
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If growth mode, retention budget likely exists — you have more room to negotiate and request off-cycle adjustments
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If cost-reduction mode, even a strong business case may hit structural budget limits — factor this into whether to pursue external options more seriously

industry_realities.common_belief: Internal promotions are fairly compensated because the company knows your value
industry_realities.actual_reality: Internal hires are systematically offered below market on the assumption they're 'already being paid' — the company anchors on your current salary plus an increment rather than market rate for the new role
industry_realities.implication: Always research and anchor on market comp for the new role level, not a percentage increase on current salary

industry_realities.common_belief: A retention counter-offer means the company truly values you and wants you to stay
industry_realities.actual_reality: Companies often make retention counter-offers knowing the employee will probably leave anyway — it buys 6–12 months to find a replacement while the employee feels valued
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate a retention offer on whether it fixes the root cause of dissatisfaction, not on the emotional signal of being wanted

industry_realities.common_belief: An internal transfer to an interesting new role is a lateral move with no real cost
industry_realities.actual_reality: Internal transfers typically reset the promotion eligibility clock, meaning a mid-cycle transfer can delay your next promotion by 2+ years while also reducing institutional knowledge capital on your current team
industry_realities.implication: Always calculate the full promo clock and equity/bonus impact before accepting a transfer, and negotiate comp increases at the time of transfer

industry_realities.common_belief: You need to wait for the annual review cycle to address a comp gap
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most companies have off-cycle market correction mechanisms that are almost never proactively offered — they exist but require the employee to explicitly request them with documented market data
industry_realities.implication: If you have clear evidence of a 15–20%+ comp gap and strong performance, don't wait for annual review — request a market correction conversation explicitly

industry_realities.common_belief: Telling your employer you have an external offer gives you leverage with no downside if you stay
industry_realities.actual_reality: Revealing that you're considering leaving permanently changes the relationship — even if you stay via counter-offer, you're now flagged as a flight risk and may be quietly deprioritized for promotions or key assignments
industry_realities.implication: Only use an external offer as internal leverage if you are genuinely prepared to take it — treat revealing it as a one-way door

industry_realities.common_belief: A manager's verbal promise of promotion is a commitment you can rely on
industry_realities.actual_reality: Verbal promotion promises are unenforceable — managers change, budgets shift, and criteria drift without written documentation; employees lose months or years waiting on promises that never materialize
industry_realities.implication: Always get promotion criteria, timeline, and comp expectations in writing before accepting any role change or continuing to wait for a promised promotion

industry_realities.common_belief: HR can always approve what a manager wants to pay
industry_realities.actual_reality: Salary bands structurally constrain what HR can approve regardless of manager intent — a manager who genuinely wants to pay you more may still be unable to do so within band limits
industry_realities.implication: Ask about salary band limits early in the negotiation to understand the structural ceiling, and factor this into whether the internal path can ever match external market

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Timing of compensation negotiation relative to promotion acceptance
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Accepts the promotion first, then tries to negotiate comp — feels that raising money before accepting would seem ungrateful or risky
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Negotiates comp explicitly before formalizing acceptance — frames it as part of clarifying the full terms of the new role
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Leverage disappears the moment you accept — senior professionals know the only negotiation window with real power is before the deal is done

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Anchors on current salary plus a percentage increase — thinks 'a 10–15% raise for a promotion seems fair'
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Anchors on market rate for the new role using external data — reframes the conversation from 'what you're getting' to 'what the role is worth'
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Current salary is an arbitrary historical number — anchoring on it systematically undervalues the new role and compounds underpayment over time

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Evaluates the retention offer primarily on the comp number — 'they matched it, so I should stay'
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Evaluates whether the root cause of dissatisfaction is genuinely resolved — asks 'would this job be worth staying for if it had always paid this?'
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Counter-offers that only address comp without fixing the underlying issue result in departure within 12 months 80% of the time

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Trusts manager relationships and takes verbal promotion promises at face value — doesn't want to seem distrustful by asking for things in writing
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Insists on written criteria, timelines, and comp terms for any commitment — treats good relationships as compatible with formal documentation
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Verbal promises have no accountability mechanism when managers change or business conditions shift — only written criteria create enforceable commitments

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Calculating the true cost of an internal transfer
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Evaluates an internal transfer on role scope and immediate comp change — doesn't think about promo clock, equity vesting, or bonus proration
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Calculates total compensation impact including promo clock reset, unvested equity impact, bonus proration, and institutional knowledge loss before deciding
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A transfer that looks neutral or positive on the surface can represent 2+ years of delayed career progression when full costs are quantified

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Using an external offer as internal leverage
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Generates an offer primarily to have something to show — isn't genuinely considering taking it and signals this by folding quickly when countered
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Only uses an external offer as leverage when genuinely willing to take it — treats the decision as real and lets that genuine optionality create authentic leverage
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A bluffed external offer signals flight risk without credible threat — it weakens future negotiations and damages internal positioning without extracting real value

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Stops interviewing externally once comfortable in a role — only goes to market when already dissatisfied, limiting negotiation leverage
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Maintains periodic external market awareness to understand real-time compensation benchmarks and keep optionality alive even when not actively considering leaving
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Internal promotion leverage is maximized when external options are real and credible — people who only go to market when pushed have less leverage than those who maintain optionality continuously
